stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, Erasmus answers, the tragedy in study
stops.campa: Erasmus, settled now at Freiburg, receives Viglius's astonished account and is not persuaded. He has spent his life arguing that memory is a plain and rational faculty, trained by ordinary method, and he has no patience for machines that promise Ciceronian eloquence by magic and Kabbalah besides. In his reply he judges that a thing capable of stirring up such excitement in the schools of Italy could produce as great a tragedy in study as Luther's had produced in religion: an old friend's fame turned, in a single letter, into a warning.

stops.name: Paris, the amphitheatre built for the king
stops.campa: By 1534 Camillo is settled at the French court, and the physician Jacques Bording writes to Étienne Dolet that Camillo has lately arrived to instruct the king and is constructing here an amphitheatre for the king, for the purpose of marking out divisions of memory. Whatever wood and glue and carved image the Venetian model amounted to, a version of it now stands, or is standing, somewhere near the French court, drawing courtiers and scholars to see the wonder that all Italy has talked of for two years.

stops.name: Paris, the lion that would not harm him
stops.campa: A story runs through the court that Camillo himself is glad to repeat. He goes one day with the Cardinal of Lorraine, the poet Luigi Alamanni, and other gentlemen to see the king's wild beasts, and a lion breaks loose and comes straight toward the party. The gentlemen scatter; Camillo, heavy-bodied and slow, alone stands his ground, less from courage, the tale-tellers admit, than from simple inability to run. The lion circles him, nuzzles him, and is driven off unharmed. All present agree it is because he stands, as his Theatre teaches, under the sign and virtue of the Sun.

stops.name: Paris, illness and the letters to Aretino
stops.campa: The years at the French court grow harder. Camillo writes often to Pietro Aretino in Venice, confessing that he is frequently ill and that the great work drags, never finished, never quite fit to be shown whole. Francis I, who once promised so much, lets the ducats come more slowly; by hint of a later letter of Erasmus to Viglius, the flow of French gold has never matched Camillo's hopes. Sometime around this year Camillo lets go of the French court for good, the Theatre still incomplete, the king's secret still ungiven, and turns back toward Italy.

stops.name: Venice, back in Italy, out of a patron
stops.campa: According to Girolamo Muzio's own account, the great man is back in Italy by 1543, his hopes at the French court exhausted, his Theatre still standing unfinished in the world's memory rather than in any one room. He is, for the first time in thirteen years, without a patron sure enough to carry the work to its end. He is over sixty, heavy, often unwell. Whatever is left of the forty-year labor Sturm will later speak of must now be gathered and given to someone, quickly, or lost with him.

stops.name: Milan, Muzio's mediation and the Marchese's offer
stops.campa: Muzio brings word of his old friend to Alfonso d'Avalos, the Marchese del Vasto, Spanish governor of Milan and commander of Charles V's armies in Italy, already patron to Ariosto and Aretino and sitter more than once for Titian's brush. The Marchese asks whether anything has come of Camillo's long hopes at the French court; hearing that it has not, he offers a pension in exchange for being taught the Theatre's secret himself. Warned by Muzio that many scholars doubt Camillo's whole enterprise, the Marchese answers simply that genuine or not, he wants it.

stops.name: Milan, the meeting with the Marchese del Vasto
stops.campa: The meeting takes place in Milan before the year turns, and it is enough to seal the arrangement: Camillo will spend what remains of his life as del Vasto's pensioner, discoursing before him and in the academies of the city. It is, the record shows, the second offer of its kind Camillo has weighed; some say the Marchese had already sounded him out as early as 1539. Now, past sixty and out of the French king's favor, Camillo accepts. The secret he swore to Francis I he has already, quietly, begun to set free.

stops.name: Milan, seven mornings in adjoining beds
stops.campa: For seven mornings, from before dawn deep into the day, Camillo dictates the outline of forty years' labor to Girolamo Muzio, the two men reclining on adjoining beds in the same room, Camillo speaking, Muzio writing down every word. Scholars will later suspect the arrangement is deliberate on Camillo's part: a memory of Solomon's own lectulum, the bed of wisdom, from which the king of Israel is said to have spoken his proverbs. What comes out of these seven mornings is the manuscript that will become, after Camillo's death, the only complete account the world will ever have of the Theatre's Idea.

stops.name: Milan, the death of Giulio Camillo
stops.campa: Soon after the seven mornings of dictation are finished, on the fifteenth of May 1544, Giulio Camillo dies in Milan. He is somewhere near sixty-four years old, by the uncertain count of his birth. The Theatre itself, the wooden object Viglius entered and touched twelve years before, has by now vanished from any record; when the French antiquary Montfaucon goes looking for it in the following century, he can find no trace. What survives is Muzio's manuscript, and the memory, already turning into legend, of the man everyone had called divine.

stops.name: Milan, burial in Santa Maria delle Grazie
stops.campa: Camillo is buried in the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie, the great Dominican church where, on the refectory wall a few steps from his grave, Leonardo's Last Supper has already been fading for forty years. The city that gave him his last patron gives him his last resting place. Within a decade admirers will be calling him a second Pico della Mirandola, a genius who died before delivering the whole fruit of a more than human intellect; within two centuries scholars will still be arguing whether the Theatre he left behind was wisdom or a beautiful, elaborate kind of confidence trick.

stops.name: Florence, L'Idea del Theatro is published
stops.campa: Six years after Camillo's death, in April 1550, the printer Lorenzo Torrentino brings out at Florence, edited by Lodovico Domenichi, the little book that is all the world will ever have of the great design: L'Idea del Theatro dell'eccellentissimo M. Giulio Camillo. Domenichi's preface admits plainly that the entire machine of so superb an edifice can no longer be found. What is printed is the outline dictated in Milan, seven mornings, two men on adjoining beds: forty years of labor folded into a pamphlet the Theatre itself would have filed away on a single gate.

stops.name: Venice, the Jubilee reprint
stops.campa: Within months, the Venetian printer Baldassar Costantini rushes out his own edition, marked on the title page as the work of the Jubilee year, l'anno del Giubileo. Seven times seven years make a Jubilee in the old law of Leviticus, and the coincidence is fitting: Camillo's Theatre was itself built seven grades by seven planets, forty-nine gates. The book that could not save the man now travels where the wooden Theatre never did: Bruno will borrow its images for his own art of shadows within a generation; Kircher's engraved theatres of knowledge and the memory palaces the Jesuits carry to Ricci's China both walk, distantly, in the room Camillo built and never finished.
